title: Codex & AI Coding Agents - Learn Agentic Coding
description:

Agentic coding is how many developers now build software: AI coding agents that read your codebase, edit multiple files, run commands and tests, and work through larger tasks with you.
 
In this hands-on course, Tom Chant, Head of Education at Scrimba, shows you how to ensure reliable results from a coding agent by giving it the right context, planning work, and controlling permissions, while verifying every change. 

You'll work through realistic tasks covering prompting, AGENTS.md, skills, testing, Git, secrets, config.toml and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This course suits experienced developers adding AI to their workflow and non-coders who wish to build software with AI help.

We'll cover:
Writing effective prompts and comment prompts for AI coding agents
Initializing projects and setting persistent instructions with AGENTS.md
Using Plan Mode to break down larger development tasks
Extending a coding agent with skills
Verifying agent changes with characterization tests and test-driven development (TDD)
Using Git safely alongside a coding agent
Keeping API keys, credentials and other secrets safe
Managing context and configuring agents with config.toml
Controlling what an agent can access and change with permissions
Connecting agents to external tools with MCP, including shadcn

title: Why Computers Can’t Count Money
description:
Ever wonder why computers struggle with basic math? This video explores a massive class of software bugs from the early 2000s that allowed people to generate real money out of thin air.

As early digital payment systems and banks rushed to digitize, engineers relied on standard floating-point numbers to process currency. However, because computers use binary (Base 2) rather than decimal (Base 10), certain fractions like $0.1$ and $0.2$ cannot be represented exactly—leading to minuscule rounding errors.

She recently helped organize TreeHacks, Stanford's annual hackathon, which narrowed 15,000 applicants down to just 1,000 participants. They built projects over a single weekend and competed for a million dollars in prizes.

Rachel grew up in Westminster, a small California town with a largely Mexican and Vietnamese population. 70% of students at her high school had family incomes so low that qualified for free school lunches. And Rachel was the first student from there to get into Stanford in years.

title: How to friction-max your learning with software engineer Jessica Rose [Podcast #216]
description:
Today Quincy Larson interviews Jessica Rose. She's a dev and teacher who's worked on open data projects at Mozilla and lots of open source projects.

We talk about:
How the whole world is hard, and how embracing that difficulty rather than avoiding it can make you a better thinker
The Bad Website club, a free online bootcamp where people learn front end development together that starts this April
Why building "silly little things" is one of the best things you can do as a learner

Bad Website Club announcement: www.freecodecamp.org/news/bad-website-club-bootcam…
Study Jess mentions about AI and worker productivity: www.raconteur.net/technology/ai-meaningful-work 

Community news section:

1. freeCodeCamp just published a new Python course that will teach you how to program your own aerial drone. You don't need to own a drone. You'll use the PySimverse simulator to practice autonomous flight. First you'll learn the basics of drone components, 3D movement, and common computer vision tasks. Then you'll learn about navigation, image capture, hand gesture control, autonomous following, and more. (2 hour YouTube course): www.freecodecamp.org/news/master-ai-drone-programm…

2. freeCodeCamp also published a massive course that will teach you how to program NVIDIA's H100 GPUs using CUDA. You'll learn about CUTLASS optimizations, multi-GPU scaling, and the primitives developers use to train large models. (24 hour YouTube course): www.freecodecamp.org/news/cuda-programming-for-nvi…

3. If you've ever wanted to build a video editor or live streaming tool that runs entirely in a browser, this handbook is worth bookmarking. You'll see how the WebCodecs API can give you low-level, hardware-accelerated control over video processing. You'll learn key concepts like video frames, codecs, containers, and muxing. (full length handbook): www.freecodecamp.org/news/the-webcodecs-handbook-n…

4. Kubernetes doesn't have a built-in user database. Instead it relies on a chain of authenticators. This course will teach you how x509 client certificates work, why they're not ideal for human users in production, and how to instead deploy your own self-hosted browser-based OpenID Connect login. (29 minute read): www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-authenticate-user…

5. The song of the week is 1983's "Oblivious" by Scottish New Wave band Aztec Camera. I love the song's Django Reinhart-style Flamenco guitars, mischevous bass line, and stereo percussion. Believe it or not, front man Roddy Frame was only 18 years old when he wrote the song, sang it, and played it's iconic guitar solo.    • Oblivious
